name: Slendo Massager

lead: The Slendo Massager was a 1940s slenderizing-salon machine that ran rollers up and down over the stomach, hips and thighs, described in period coverage as a way to rub away fat from those areas. It belongs to a mid-century trend of passive reducing machines that promised a slimmer figure without exercise.

A 1940s LIFE photograph by Alfred Eisenstaedt shows a model using the machine at a New York salon. Related machines in that era included barrel, ring and leg rollers [1]. No published studies of the Slendo itself are known, and similar vibrating devices were widely marketed through the 1960s before declining by the 1980s [2].

paras: Clients used salon sessions where an attendant or the user moved the rollers across targeted areas such as hips, abdomen and thighs. Machines were part of a salon routine alongside other roller devices.

No specific safety data are published for the Slendo. Roller and vibration massage can cause temporary skin redness or soreness; people with medical conditions are usually advised by clinicians to ask before using vibrating devices.

chain: Temporary skin and tissue effects, passive 'spot reduction' claims
angle.text: Marketed as a way to reduce fat on hips, stomach and thighs through rolling massage. Any immediate effect comes from massage itself; fat reduction was the advertised, untested claim.

lead: The Slendo Massager was a 1940s machine used in slenderizing salons, described as running rollers up and down to electrically rub away fat from the stomach, hips and thighs [1]. Its coiled-spring roller design was marketed for passive spot reduction, meaning a slimmer-looking figure without exercise.

It appears in a 1940s LIFE photograph by Alfred Eisenstaedt showing model Pat Ogden using it in a New York slenderizing salon, a fad described as the newest in fitness at the time; other machines there included a roller for the abdomen, a barrel massager for hips and buttocks, a back ring roller and leg rollers [1].

Related vibrating belt machines, tracing to Gustav Zander's late-nineteenth-century massage devices and John Harvey Kellogg's 1927 'Health Builder', were sold in the 1950s to passively reduce fat, remained popular through the 1960s and fell out of fashion by the 1980s [2].
infobox: Vibrating belt machines, barrel and ring rollers

paras: Period descriptions portray a cage of coiled springs or rollers moved along the body so as to massage targeted areas [1]. The machines were used in salons as part of a menu of roller devices for different body zones [1].

The Slendo sits within the wider history of mechanical massagers sold for slimming. Vibrating belt machines were promoted as breaking up abdominal fat by vibration, featured in television comedy of the 1950s and 1960s, and had declined by the 1980s; the Wikipedia article states they were found to have no fat-reducing benefit [2].
